1:
Keil and Delitzsch open by pairing the nations: the Ammonites were the twin people of the Moabites not only in descent but in character and in their relation to Israel, and from them too the Amorite king had wrenched a portion of territory which Israel received when he was subdued — territory they sought every opportunity to take back. Ellicott traces the same rivalry through a longer series of attempts to recover the lost ground that failed under the judges and under two later kings and succeeded only after the tribes beyond Jordan were deported. Calvin goes further back still, to a descent from Lot that he calls base and shameful, being the offspring of incest,, noting that God spared both peoples for that man's sake when he brought Israel out of Egypt, so that their ingratitude doubled the crime.

Henry casts the opening verse as a lawsuit. An action is brought in God's name against the Ammonites for an illegal encroachment on the rightful possessions of the tribe next to them,. Does the estate escheat for want of an heir? Are there no Gadites left to whom the inheritance belongs, or, failing them, none of Judah nearer of kin than these intruders? And Henry presses the worst count: there were heirs of their own body yet unborn whom the Ammonites, to forestall the claim, barbarously murdered. Wesley states the principle more plainly, that God had given Gilead to three tribes, and that as men's estates ought to descend to their heirs so this land should have descended to their posterity. Gill notes only that the heading will bear to be rendered concerning them, or to them, or against them.

Calvin then explains why the sentence is dated rather than immediate. God testifies that he would not suffer them to enjoy their unjust plunder for ever, but the prediction was uttered while they were secure, and some years passed in which they still held their spoils; the faithful are deliberately held in suspense so that they may learn to wait patiently for the fixed time. Calvin also pauses over the manner of the threat, defending the prophets' elevated style: had they spoken without metaphor and simply narrated their matter, their words would have been frigid and inefficient and would never have penetrated men's hearts,. Ellicott supplies the city itself — the capital, whose full and formal title meant the great city of waters —. Clarke dates the whole collection to the ministry of Nebuchadnezzar during the thirteen years' siege of Tyre.

Three details are contested. Whose city Heshbon was: Gill calls it a city of Moab lying on the Ammonite border, and reports the inference drawn from this verse that the Ammonites were destroyed before the Moabites, as well as the suggestion that Heshbon was a double city divided by a river with one side belonging to each people; Ellicott says it was strictly an Ammonite city despite its earlier appearance among Moab's fortunes, and Keil and Delitzsch draw from the summons the inference that the former royal residence was then in Ammonite hands. Which Ai is meant: Ellicott says it is obviously not the town near Jericho, so that unless the text is corrupt we must infer a city of the same name beyond Jordan, and Wesley agrees it cannot be the one taken in the conquest. And what the hedges are: Clarke offers the walls by which the dead were commonly buried, or else the villages called the daughters of the capital, whose people are told to seek safety elsewhere; Ellicott replies that hedges in the English sense have never been common in the East,, the word meaning the palings of sheepfolds or the walls of vineyards and never a city wall.
4:
What the valleys are divides Calvin from everyone else. Gill takes them for the fertile and well-watered vales lying by the two border rivers, including the plain of the vineyards, and adds that the whole country was really a vale, since the historian places both Moab and Ammon in the hollow Syria named from its low situation between the two Lebanon ranges; their glorying was in the produce of these valleys, the grass and corn and vines and the flocks that fed there. Keil and Delitzsch say the same more briefly, that the boast was of splendid fruitful plains which, being well watered, produced large crops. Ellicott thinks the word exactly describes the conformation of the country as a high plateau cut by streams running down toward the Jordan. Clarke simply warns against the boast: though the valleys be fruitful, glory not in them, nor in political and military power, nor in a multitude of cities, for a stronger is coming. Calvin dissents. Some understand a fertile and watered land, he says, but he takes the word for fortified places instead, since the people were ringed by mountains and thought themselves unapproachable; and the flowing he refers to the look of a region set among mountains, which seems to run down like a river.

Ellicott offers two renderings of the disputed phrase and lets both stand: thy valley that floweth with plenty, or else thy valley floweth away, that is, is wasted and emptied. He also finds something suggestive in the title given to Ammon here, since it is the epithet the same prophet had earlier applied to the northern kingdom, and he supposes Ammon too had known the opportunity of worshipping the God of Israel and had probably taken it up for as long as Israelites were her rulers.

On the terror threatened, Calvin sets the sentence out as a deliberate opposition. Fear is raised against the security in which the Ammonites lay torpid, inebriated as it were with their pleasures, their strongholds having so hardened their hearts that they feared no danger at all; and the clause about being driven out every man straight before him is added because they reckoned that with so many outlets they could always slip away on one side or another if an enemy pressed them. Gill identifies the fear concretely with the Chaldean army, which would strike a panic into men who thought themselves secure in their fortresses and trusted in their riches. Wesley glosses the two hard phrases, that they shall be glad to flee and never look back, and that none will receive or entertain the wanderer.

The closing promise of restoration divides them along a different line. Gill and Clarke look for a historical return, Clarke supposing the Ammonites came back with the Moabites and the Israelites on the permission given by the edict of Cyrus, and Gill naming the same deliverer and observing that by the days of Judas Maccabeus the children of Ammon were once more a large and mighty people. Calvin and Wesley look past that. Wesley thinks the words probably refer to the conversion of the Ammonites, with other heathen, to Christ. Calvin says the same at more length and with a careful qualification: such promises were adventitious, since God had chosen one people only and had built a wall to separate them from aliens, yet it was his will to give preludes of his favour and of the calling of the Gentiles, so that the prophet here has regard to the kingdom of Christ and the promise extends to his coming. Keil and Delitzsch, characteristically, report what is known of the event instead, that the historian records a defeat and subjugation of the Ammonites in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem.
7:
Calvin fixes on the kinship as the aggravation: the Idumeans had descended from the same father as the chosen people, gloried in their holy descent, so that their bitter hatred toward their own blood was a most impious cruelty. Wesley tells the story from Esau, disinherited when the blessing went to the younger brother, yet promised a fat and plentiful country and a yoke he would one day break,. Ellicott gives the political sequence — conquest under Saul and more completely under David, a failed revolt under Solomon, a successful one under Joram, attempts by two later kings to reassert dominion, an invasion of Judah under Ahaz, and independence by the reign of Zedekiah. Henry adds the motive for recording the doom at all: these old enemies had triumphed over Israel and rejoiced in her calamity so the sentence stands as comfort to Israel as well as warning to Edom.

Gill reports two readings he will not take. The rabbinic interpreters he cites refer the prophecy to a destruction still future, that of Rome, Edom being with the Jews a common name for it; another expositor holds that the Jews themselves are meant, since the Idumeans were incorporated with them before the coming of Christ and an Idumean reigned over them. Gill judges it best to understand the prophecy properly and literally of the Idumeans. Clarke marks the passage as a new and separate discourse and takes Teman for a part of Idumea standing for the whole country. Calvin reads the opening question as irony: though they thought themselves safe through their own counsels it would avail nothing, since the Lord would blind them and deprive them of a sane mind.

The relation to Obadiah is disputed, and the direction of borrowing with it. Calvin says interpreters have not merely obscured but perverted the passage and gone far from the meaning, because it did not occur to them to compare Obadiah, who is the true interpreter and from whom our prophet has borrowed; and since Obadiah came first, he had to speak of the thing as future, whereas this prophet, the judgment being near, boldly exults over the Idumeans. Henry agrees the expressions are borrowed, and accounts for the harmony by observing that all the prophets were inspired by one and the same Spirit. Keil and Delitzsch call it a reproduction, but note a change: what the earlier prophet brings forward as a comparison is here applied directly to the enemy, who are themselves the grape-gatherers leaving nothing and the night thieves destroying till they have enough. They add a caution against Calvin's kind of harmonising, insisting the following clauses are not to be taken as questions and that the parallel does not entitle anyone to import the interrogative particle from it. Ellicott, by contrast, speaks of the words as reproduced in Obadiah.

On the flight, Clarke finds an allusion to the custom of the Arabs, who on the approach of a powerful foe strike their tents, lade their camels within a couple of hours and bury themselves in a desert where no enemy can follow. Gill has them hiding in deep caverns and the dens of rocks, and reports the division over Dedan, which he takes for another city of Idumea though some make it an Arabian country bordering on Edom and subdued by the Edomites. Ellicott notes that Dedan appears elsewhere in company with Edom and Teman and carried Edom's traffic with other countries,. Wesley draws the comparison out: the destruction will not be like a gleaning, where gatherers content themselves with the principal clusters, nor like the robbing of thieves, who take what serves their hunger and leave the rest. Ellicott closes with a silence he thinks significant — there is no promise anywhere that Edom's captivity should be brought back.
10:
Gill and Clarke read the stripping plainly: the Chaldeans took away cities, castles, villages, people, wealth and treasure, and the hiding-places were discovered to the enemy so that no defence remained. Calvin adds a gloss and an inference. By the hidden things he understands treasures, as he says is evident from Obadiah, and takes the sense to be that God would so expose the Idumeans to plunder that nothing concealed would escape seizure. That, he argues, confirms the point of the previous comparison: this would not be like a grape-gathering, or a theft, or a common robbery, because God meant to empty them altogether of everything they had. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the text of the sentence, which leaves the seed spoiled together with the brethren and the neighbours, and the man himself simply not there.

The next verse then divides them sharply, and the question is whether it is mercy or irony. Gill hears it first as the kind of thing a man says when he must flee or is at the point of death, committing his family to a friend who promises them food and raiment, which serves to make him easy — and then observes that there would be no Edomites left to say such kind words or do so friendly a part. He reports as well that some take the words as God's own, spoken either ironically or seriously, and suggesting that there would be neither children nor widows left to leave behind. His own verdict comes in the following verse, where he says the preceding words are not spoken by way of promise and comfort but of threatening.

Clarke goes the other way without hesitation. He grants that the connection with the context is not easy to discern, but takes the sentence as a maxim of great importance in itself: widows and orphans are the peculiar care of God, who is the best of fathers to the one and the most loving of husbands to the other, so that even the widows and orphans of Esau who survive the general destruction will be cared for by the Lord. Ellicott poses the alternatives explicitly and then chooses. Were the words uttered in the stern irony of a man who veils a threat in the form of a promise, as some have thought, or was there even in Edom's case a mingling of pity for the helpless? The second seems to him truer to this prophet's character, and he adds that if the sentence passed left the wives of Edom widows and their children orphans, God had still not forgotten that he was the God of the widow and the fatherless.

On the cup they converge again. Ellicott takes the imagery up from an earlier chapter of the same book and states the argument as one from the greater to the less: even those who might have seemed exempted by God's own decree from drinking his wrath had drunk it, so Esau could hardly hope for immunity — a thought he finds parallel to the apostle's saying that judgment begins at the house of God. Wesley names the drinkers outright as the Jews, who in comparison with others did not deserve the cup and yet drank it, and puts the conclusion as a rule: when an Israelite has not escaped the justice of God, an Edomite must not expect to. Clarke reaches the same end by the same road, noting that the form of speech occurs elsewhere in the book, and asking whether one who is worse than those already punished can expect to escape.
13:
Gill explains the oath by the nature of the swearer and of the thing sworn: God swore by himself because he could swear by no greater, and he swore at all because the event was so extraordinary that it was scarcely thought credible. On the city named, Clarke and Wesley agree that Bozrah stands as a part for the whole country, being its principal city; Ellicott identifies it as one of the chief cities of Edom and probably the modern El-Busaireh, half-way between Petra and the Dead Sea.

What the herald is divides them. Calvin refuses the ordinary rendering: some say a report, he thinks improperly, for although the word often means a report or rumour it ought here to be taken for a proclamation which God published by his own heralds, the figure being drawn from men proclaiming war. Ellicott reads it the same way, with the Lord as the great King sending out his envoy to summon the nations against Edom. Clarke will not have an envoy at all, holding that the words mean only that God gave permission and stirred up the hearts of these nations against a people already doomed. Wesley takes a middle course, allowing that the prophet speaks after the manner of earthly princes who send ambassadors to declare their minds, while making the substance of it that God inclined them to come. Gill keeps to the hearing itself, a report of Edom's destruction made to the prophet in a dream or vision by the spirit of prophecy.

Calvin then reports and declines the majority reading of the sentence that follows. Interpreters mostly take it that the people would be made contemptible because God had determined to cast them from the dignity they had for a time enjoyed, and they connect the next verse as giving the reason. The passage may be taken otherwise, Calvin says, as God deriding a pride which ought to have restrained itself because it contended against nature in wishing to elate itself so far; and this seems to him the real meaning, though he is careful not to pronounce the other wrong. Gill reports a different division on the same clause, between those who make it describe what Edom was at the first, a people few in number with no large country, and his own view that it describes what Edom was to become, which was the reason for gathering the Chaldeans against them. Ellicott corrects only the rendering, preferring among the nations to among the heathen since no contrast with Israel is intended here.

The word rendered terribleness draws the closest attention. Gill notes that some render it thine idol, since the root means to be formidable and to cause trembling, as the idols of the Gentiles were to their worshippers; he observes that the Latin version interprets the cognate word elsewhere of Priapus, an image set up in gardens to frighten off birds and thieves, and that one rabbinic commentator reports an interpretation of it here as idolatrous worship. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by his own route: the noun occurs nowhere else, and though etymologically it might mean terror of or object of terror, a cognate is used elsewhere for an idol probably of that same type, which is likely the sense — the thing being called scornfully the horror of Edom, just as the God of Israel was called the fear of Isaac. He supports it with Milton, who names the god of Moab the obscene dread of that people's sons. Of the dwelling in the clefts, Ellicott prefers in the fortresses of Sela, while Clarke keeps the plain geography, that all Idumea is full of mountains and rocks and the rocks full of caves, where in great heats and in time of war the people take shelter.
17:
Calvin explains the repetition rather than the content: the prophet says again what he has said because nobody could have thought the destruction so near, and the point of saying it twice is not to clear an obscurity but to fix in the hearts of the faithful a thing that looked incredible. On the hissing he allows two senses and refuses to choose, since many hiss or shake the head in mockery while others hiss from wonder when something unusual happens. Gill states the extent of it plainly, that not the chief city only but the whole country would be laid waste, its fortified towns destroyed, its riches plundered and its people killed or carried off.

The comparison with the overthrown cities is pressed by all of them. Gill takes the point to be suddenness and completeness, nothing left and nobody spared. Clarke observes that the ruin of those cities had become the standard of terror, so that when God threatens incorrigible sinners he tells them they shall be like them, and he presses the clause about no man abiding there into a distinction: travellers may lodge on the ground for a night, but the place cannot become a permanent dwelling. Ellicott finds the notable thing elsewhere, in the mention of the neighbour cities, which he connects with their being named in the law as Admah and Zeboim. Calvin draws the conclusion that no hope remained, the overthrow being inevitable because God meant them wholly destroyed and their memory obliterated.

Calvin then qualifies himself in a way worth setting beside Ellicott's history. It is probable, he grants, that some remnant of the nation survived; but this is not inconsistent with the prophecy, because those who remained alive were so scattered that they never again formed one people. Ellicott supplies the evidence from the other end. The words received no immediate or even rapid fulfilment: Idumea was a populous and powerful country in the time of John Hyrcanus, and Petra was rebuilt by the Romans as a centre of trade and government with its baths and theatres and temples. But the end came at last, and there are few lands once the seat of a thriving nation more utterly desolate than this one, which disappears from history altogether from the ninth Christian century.

The lion of the last verse produces a genuine division over who is meant. Gill reports that the Targum rightly understands it of a king and his army. Clarke agrees and names the chosen man as Nebuchadnezzar, whom God has selected and commissioned against Idumea; he quotes an expositor who paraphrases the whole as God saying that when he raises such a commotion in the country as a fierce lion makes in the sheepfolds, he will cause the man to run away from her as affrighted shepherds and their flocks run from a lion. Ellicott builds the same picture from the words, preferring the pride of Jordan to the swelling of Jordan for the thick jungle-forests that were the glory of its banks, and the evergreen pasturage to the habitation of the strong, since the second noun conveys permanence rather than strength; the image is then a lion working through the jungle and rushing on the flocks in one of the meadow tracts along the river. Wesley alone reverses the parts, making it the Edomites who come up fiercely against the invader and then flee suddenly, even out of their own country; and he reads the closing questions as a challenge nobody can take up, since God can do whatever he pleases and no potentate will stand before him.
20:
Whether Teman is simply another name for Edom is disputed. Clarke treats it as taken here for the whole of Idumea, one of a set of synonyms that prevent monotony and give variety to the poet's versification, and Wesley says flatly that Edom and Teman signify the same thing. Keil and Delitzsch deny it: Teman is not synonymous with Edom, and its inhabitants are named separately in the parallel member because they were particularly famous for the wisdom the oracle opened by mocking. Gill passes over the question and takes the counsel to be the decree, the purpose God had formed in his heart against the Idumeans, wisely framed and on just grounds.

The clause about the least of the flock divides them further. Clarke makes the Edomites the sheep — they shall be like timid sheep, and the weakest foe will overcome them. Wesley keeps the same sense but transfers the smallness to the other side, so that the least of the invader's forces will drag them out of their hiding places. Ellicott calls the English obscure and diagnoses why: the object of the verb has probably been taken for its subject. He would render it that the invaders will vex them, the feeble ones of the flock, and will make their pasturage terror-stricken at them — the thought being that the very fields of Edom would shudder at the cruelty of their conquerors. He adds two observations of his own, that the word rendered surely is literally if not, the strongest Hebrew idiom of asseveration, and that the whole passage recurs later in the book, where it is applied to Babylon instead.

On the noise of the fall they enlarge in much the same direction. Gill reads it as a fall from the height of greatness to a very low condition, notes that the higher the thing falls from the greater the noise it makes, and suspects an allusion to the falling of the rocks and hills in which that country abounded; the noise itself he leaves open between the shout of the conquerors, the cry of the Edomites and the report of the disaster spreading through the world. Clarke pictures the whole state as a vast building suddenly thrown down, so that the earth trembles and the crash is heard at a great distance, and Calvin uses the same image of a great mass falling and shaking the ground, his point being that the fall of a people who had long gloried in their wealth could not but strike all their neighbours with terror. Ellicott fixes the place, rendering the sea literally the Weedy or Reed sea and noting that Edom's own port lay on the gulf that washed those shores.

The closing figure changes the animal. Ellicott observes that the prophet passes from one symbol of sovereignty to another, the lion giving way to the eagle, and that what one city had been to Moab in an earlier oracle Bozrah is to Edom here, its capture painted in the same terms. Clarke names the eagle as Nebuchadnezzar. Calvin makes the point that the comparison is chosen for speed and ruin together, and then supplies the circumstance that gives the threat its force: at the time this was spoken nobody could have suspected the Chaldeans would ever become enemies to the Idumeans, since the two were on the best of terms and the Edomites took every care to keep their favour. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the eagle image is carried on in the words for coming up, which do not describe the bird rising into the air.
23:
Henry sets the geography: the kingdom of Syria lay north of Canaan as Edom lay south, and Damascus being its metropolis the ruin of the whole is supposed in the ruin of that city. Gill and Wesley agree that the capital stands for the country. Clarke and Ellicott supply the history from opposite ends of it — Clarke tracing the city's capture by David, its recovery of independence under Solomon's successor and its long wars with the northern kingdom, until a king of Judah leagued with Assyria, whose army besieged and demolished it; Ellicott beginning with the kingdom's rise to power after David's death and ending with the memorable confederacy of two kings which ended, as an earlier prophet foretold, in subjugation by the Assyrians. Wesley glosses the trouble on the sea as the distress of those who live near it.

The exclamation over the city divides them three ways. Calvin reports that some think the possessive redundant and render it simply the city of joy, the versions mostly doing so and treating the letter as paragogic; they are moved, he thinks, by no good reason, having found it absurd that the prophet should call Damascus a city of joy to himself when he owed it no love. But prophets do not always speak according to their own feelings and often assume the persons of others, so the words may stand as they are, and on that reading the prophet exults very cuttingly. Wesley makes the speaker explicit and supposes the Syrian king is the one lamenting. Ellicott hears neither the prophet nor the king but an exclamation half scornful and half ironical, pointing back to the failed flight of the inhabitants: the city so fair and glorious with its two rivers had not been left, and would not be found empty when taken, since the people were to perish inside it.

Gill adds what made the place worth an exclamation, its antiquity, wealth, strength and reputation for devotion even among the heathen; Clarke reduces the sentence to its result, that Damascus is so ruined she can no longer be called a praiseworthy or happy city. On the particle that opens the next verse Gill and Calvin converge against a common reading. Calvin notes that the Hebrews take it as assigning a reason, so that the cause of the decree would be the city's long war against Israel and then against the Jews and its unceasing persecution of the Church; he prefers the simpler sense of a plain affirmative, which the word carries in many other places. Gill reaches the same place from the other side, rendering it verily and reporting the interpretation that makes it an oath, God swearing that so it should be.

The palaces named at the close draw out the antiquarians. Clarke says only that the name was common to several of the Syrian kings. Keil and Delitzsch take the palaces for those of the Syrian kings generally on that ground,. Ellicott counts three kings of the name in the history, the last of them of a different dynasty from the other two, thinks later kings may have borne it too since it was bound up with the kingdom's greatness, and notes that it appears in the Assyrian inscriptions in a slightly different form. Henry reports the derivation that makes it the son of Hadad, either their idol or one of their ancient kings. On the fire, Gill offers a literal option, that the houses built upon the wall were set alight by the Chaldeans, or else that a breach was made there at which the destruction began; Calvin takes it as metaphor throughout, since no fire was applied to the walls and palaces, the figure being chosen because nothing is more violent or dreadful and the greatest cities are soon reduced to ashes when it begins to blaze.
28:
On Kedar there is no dispute. All of them derive the name from a son of Ishmael whose posterity settled in Arabia the Stony; Clarke and Ellicott add that the tribe was known for supplying the markets of Tyre with cattle, sheep and goats,. Keil and Delitzsch describe them as a Bedouin nation dwelling in tents. Hazor is another matter, and the voices divide four ways. Gill identifies it with Petra itself, the metropolis whose king had several petty kings under him, and denies it can be the Hazor destroyed by Joshua in Canaan. Wesley makes exactly that identification, calling Hazor the head city of several kingdoms in Joshua's time. Henry takes a middle road that Gill also reports as an opinion of others, supposing the people were originally Canaanites of the northern kingdom that had Jabin for its king, who were driven out, settled in the Arabian deserts and associated themselves with the Kedarenes. Ellicott doubts it is a city at all: the name belongs to many places in Palestine, but its combination with Kedar points to quite another region, and he thinks the prophet probably uses it of a district, as a similar word is used elsewhere for the villages of Kedar. Clarke simply confesses defeat and says he cannot find the place, which was no doubt in Arabia and of considerable importance but is now no more.

The way of life is described with unusual agreement and unusual detail. Calvin observes that the mention of tents and curtains is fitted to the nation: the Arabs dwelt in cabins and tents, as they still do, and were shepherds with no cultivated fields, leading their flocks through the deserts and keeping a great number of camels, so that they had neither cities nor palaces nor much wealth of any other kind. Gill notes that they were called Scenites from their tents and Nomads from their wandering; Clarke draws the same conclusion from the inventory of plunder, that the list of tents, flocks, curtains and camels identifies them as tent-dwelling Arabs whose principal property was cattle.

Henry makes the description into a portrait of a whole manner of living, very different from that of the nations round about them. They dwelt in tents and had curtains instead of walls, no fortified cities, neither gates nor bars; being shepherds they had no treasure but their stock upon the land and no money but flocks and camels; they kept no soldiers because they feared no invader, and had no merchants because they dwelt alone, so that they lived within themselves, content with the products and pleasures of their own country. What follows, he observes, is that they were nevertheless rich.

On the last two verses the comment turns to method. Ellicott hears in the cry of terror on every side a striking individuality, since it reproduces the very phrase that had been so prominent in this prophet's own life and preaching. Wesley identifies the plunderers briefly as the Chaldeans, and Clarke reads the command to dwell deep as it was read of Dedan earlier, a summons to retire into the depths of the desert; Ellicott adds that the dwellers in the villages of Hazor are told to flee into the furthest recesses of the wilderness, and dates the words after the battle of Carchemish, when the conqueror established his sovereignty over the lower Euphrates, northern Arabia and the Syrian desert. Calvin fixes on the counsel and the purpose taken against them, and takes both words to mean the secret means by which the king subdued a people who feared nothing of the kind: while these shepherds lived securely on their mountains he prepared his forces and divided them, so that they were taken by craft rather than by strength.
31:
Three of them reject the received rendering of the nation's epithet, and for the same reason. Gill would have it the nation that is at ease rather than the wealthy nation, meaning a people living quietly and in peace, with no wars against their neighbours and none among themselves, and he supports the change with a plain observation: the Kedarenes were not a very wealthy people. Clarke renders it simply the peaceable nation. Calvin notes that the word means delicate in other places but here means secure, and insists the point is not enjoyment but the absence of fear, since though there might be no joys among them theirs was a nation that dreaded nothing; the clauses that follow, about having neither gates nor bars and dwelling alone, he takes as the prophet explaining his own epithet. Clarke supplies the same explanation from the manner of life, that the Arabs had nothing but their tents, no cities and not even permanent villages.

Who gives the order to go up is disputed between two of them. Wesley makes it the outcome of Nebuchadrezzar's deliberations, the king charging his armies to march against a people who lived at ease, took no care, and had no neighbours able to come to their aid. Gill denies this outright. The words do not express the counsel and purpose of the king, he says, nor are they his address to his army; they are the words of the Lord, and it is the Lord who commissions both the king and his forces to go up in hostile fashion against the Kedarenes.

On the scattering, Calvin finds an implied comparison in the language. It sometimes happens that a country is plundered while the inhabitants, stripped of their goods, stay where they are and live on in poverty; here the words are emphatic, and they set the people against chaff, so that as chaff is driven in every direction by gusts of wind, so would this people be dispersed. Clarke takes the phrase about the utmost corners geographically, citing an expositor who reads it of insulated coasts and the peninsula of Arabia, and presses the point that even in those inaccessible recesses the sword and the pillage would find them out. Keil and Delitzsch note that the camels and the multitude of cattle are named as booty because they were the whole of the plunder such a people could furnish.

The closing sentence on Hazor draws a comment from Calvin on prophetic idiom. The prophets often say of a land deserted by its inhabitants that it will become the habitation of dragons, and he explains why: this is more grievous than the land merely standing empty, for when dragons succeed men the thing is dreadful, and the image is chosen so that the judgment of God may make a deeper impression on men's feelings. Keil and Delitzsch render the creatures jackals and take the dwellings of the settled tribes to be meant. Gill applies it to the royal city where the king and the principal men had lived, now to be inhabited by wild beasts instead. On how long the desolation lasts they differ slightly: Clarke says it is never to be repeopled, and that though the place may occasionally be visited it can never be made a permanent abode, while Gill allows the perpetuity to mean at least a very long time, and Calvin pauses over the word for perpetuity itself.
34:
Who the Elamites were is the standing question, and the answers spread widely. Wesley says probably the Persians, and Henry agrees, descending them from a son of Shem while allowing that some restrict the name to the part of Persia nearest the Jews. Gill reports the common identification with Persia but prefers the country of Elymais, distinct from both Persia and Media although later absorbed into the Persian empire. Clarke is blunter: some think Elam always means Persia, but this is not at all likely, since it was part of the Babylonian empire in Daniel's time and is most probably the Elymais of the Greeks. Calvin goes furthest of all. He would rather say the Elamites were the Parthians, were it not that an evangelist lists the two as distinct peoples, and he offers a reason for rejecting Persia that none of the others gives: the Persians were remote from the Jews and had never injured them, so there was no occasion for a prophet to denounce punishment on them.

The date attached to this oracle is itself discussed, since Ellicott observes that it is the only one in these two chapters to carry one. Assuming it correctly given, he says, it puts this oracle later than those before it; but many critics have argued the opposite, holding that the absence of the conqueror's name, so prominent elsewhere after the deportation, points to an earlier date instead. Keil and Delitzsch accept the heading and draw the consequence that this utterance was published after the surrounding oracles and not long before the one concerning Babylon. Clarke takes the date to sever rather than to place it, concluding that a prophecy delivered at the beginning of that reign can have no natural or historical connection with the others gathered in this various chapter. Henry, by contrast, uses it to date the neighbours, thinking it probable that the preceding prophecies against the Gentiles belong to the same time.

On the bow they are unanimous and well supplied. Gill notes the Elamites were famous for skill in archery and that the Targum renders the phrase their strength. Clarke says they had acquired their power and eminence by dexterity with the bow,. Ellicott adds the account of the three things taught to the youth of Persia — to ride, to draw the bow, and to speak the truth. Calvin generalises instead: every nation possesses its own peculiar excellency in war; light infantry was once in repute among the Italians and the Gauls excelled in mailed horsemen, and though all things are changed now, every nation still differs in its art of war. Henry draws a moral from the breaking of it, that God often orders matters so that what we most trust to fails us first, and the chief of our might proves the least of our help.

The four winds are read two ways. Gill and Clarke take them for armies. Gill reports the Targum's rendering of them as four kingdoms and the opinion that the words were accomplished under Alexander or his four successors, but prefers the Chaldean invasion, whose army drew men from several quarters of the world, and Clarke adds that the scattered would be spread through all the provinces of that empire. Keil and Delitzsch read the figure theologically, holding that wind is the most appropriate of earthly things for symbolising the Spirit of God or the energy of the divine operation. Ellicott keeps the picture agricultural, noticing that the words repeat an earlier verse of this chapter as to the extent of the scattering but add a circumstance of terror, the winds now whirling round as in a cyclone, so that the threshing-floor is before us again and the Elamites are the chaff carried off in every direction.
37:
Calvin draws an inference from the severity itself. This verse especially shows, he says, that the Elamites were among those who had raged inhumanly against God's people, since such vengeance would not have been set forth without cause; they must have been among the chief of his enemies, or at the least cruel in no ordinary way and delighting in slaughter. He also weighs the verb of the first clause, which means to tear in pieces, and objects to those who render it I will lay prostrate as missing the difference. Gill keeps to the effect, a panic so complete that they would have neither heart nor spirit to go out and meet the enemy or defend themselves, but would make all the haste imaginable to flee. Keil and Delitzsch simply set the three verses out together.

The throne divides them. Gill takes it as God's own, so called because he gave it to the conqueror, and notes that his palace, like that of his successors, was probably at Shushan within Elam. Wesley says the same of a different king, that God calls the throne of Cyrus or Alexander his because he gave it to the conqueror; Clarke leaves the choice open between the two rulers while observing that Cyrus certainly made himself master of Elymais and Media. Ellicott states the principle behind the phrase: the throne of the Lord is the throne of whichever king is for the time his chosen instrument and servant, which here means the Chaldean, against whom Elam seems to have risen in rebellion. Calvin alone declines to make it a royal seat at all, and reads it as a tribunal: God would avenge himself as though his court were erected in that land. He adds the qualification that God is said to erect his throne wherever he rules, and that his kingdom is not always to be taken in a good sense.

What the consumption leaves is a further question. Calvin holds that though some individuals would remain alive the name of the people would not survive and the race as such would become extinct — which makes his comment on the closing promise the more striking.

For that promise all four who treat it read the latter days christologically, though by different routes and with different confidence. Gill rules out the obvious candidate on chronology: the liberty the Elamites enjoyed under Cyrus cannot properly be called the latter days so the times of the Messiah must be meant. Clarke reaches the same conclusion more tentatively, thinking it probably means the spiritual freedom given under the gospel, while noting that under Cyrus the Elamites were gathered from all quarters and united with the Persians as masters of the east — and he confesses that difficulties remain, since who the Elamites were is still a question, his own best answer being that they and the Persians were two distinct peoples afterwards blended. Wesley allows both senses to stand, the words meaning either after many days, in which case they may refer to Cyrus, or the time of the Messiah, in which case they refer to the spiritual liberty some of these heathen were brought into; and he supplies the evidence that Elamites were at Jerusalem at Pentecost and were among those converted. Calvin is the frankest of them. If it be asked when this was fulfilled, he answers that no restoration of that nation is recorded in history at all; the prophet is giving the Elamites the hope he had given other nations, that they should be united again under Christ as their head, so that although the Elamites were never afterwards known, the promise was not made in vain.
